1:
Bede and Robertson take the word for treasury apart the same way, as a compound of the Persian term for a royal hoard with the Greek for keeping or guarding; Bede adds the furniture, a chest with an opening at the top set near the altar on the right hand of those entering, into which the priests put what was given for the temple, and Robertson that the noun is common in the Greek Old Testament but occurs in the New only here, in the parallel and in one place in John. Robertson also supplies the hour. The debate was over and the council had withdrawn in defeat; the seated teacher watching the rich put in their gifts is taking, he says, a slight diversion from the strain of the preceding hours. Gill notices a smaller thing, that the treasury cannot have stood above him since he was directly opposite it, and reports that three of the versions omit the clause about looking up altogether. Bede draws the moral of the watching before any of the giving is described: the same Lord who overthrew those who traded in his house also marks those who bring gifts to it, praising the deserving and condemning the rest.

The word chosen for the woman's poverty is not the usual one, and Robertson and Ellicott arrive independently at the same conclusion about why. Robertson derives it from the verb to work for one's living and notes it is kin to the word for being hungry and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, while the parallel gospel uses a commoner term built on cowering and hiding from fear, the proper word for beggary. Ellicott reaches the distinction from the other end, holding the rarer word carefully chosen to say that the widow, though needy and driven to work for a scanty maintenance, was not a beggar. Clarke takes the opposite view of the force of the term, rendering it miserably poor and arguing that the depth of the poverty is what heightens the merit of what she did. On the coins themselves he is expansive: two of them made the fourth part of the Roman penny, and though that quarter-piece was the smallest brass coin at Rome a smaller one circulated among the Jews, named from a verb meaning to fail.

Clarke then follows the English words back rather than the Greek. Our penny was once struck with a deep indented cross dividing it into four, so that broken in two it made the halfpenny and broken in four the fourthing, which we have corrupted into farthing; and mite he derives either from the creature our ancestors took for the smallest of animals or from the Latin for a small thing, whence the French word for a crumb. Ellicott notes two smaller points of text, that the evangelist writes truly where the parallel has Amen, which he thinks characteristic, and that the better manuscripts drop the closing words about the offerings of God. Henry asks why the story is told twice and answers that charity to the poor is a main matter in religion; he adds a sharper reason, that the scribes who devoured widows' houses had just been named, and that it aggravates the charge if the poor widows were the best benefactors of the funds those men administered. He presses the watching as a warning and a comfort at once: the eye that saw her sees whether we give in proportion to what we have or are paltry in it, and whether we give willingly or grudgingly, and men may satisfy themselves with excuses he knows to be frivolous. Gill puts the consolation plainly, that mean services done in faith and love are preferred before greater ones in which both are wanting.
5:
What the disciples admired is described more fully by the sources than by the text. Barnes takes the goodly stones either of the large squared blocks of the eastern wall or of precious stones used in decorating the building itself, and Clarke allows the same two possibilities. Robertson reports that some of the stones in the substructure were enormous and that the columns of the portico were single blocks of marble over forty feet high; Wesley gives measurements from a man who had lately measured them, five cubits high and six broad and forty-five long, and adds that they had been brought from another country and that no engine then in use could have lifted them. He describes the effect as well, marble so white that at a distance the building looked like a mountain of snow, and gilding that made it a splendid spectacle when the sun struck it. On the gifts, Barnes explains the practice by the older custom of hanging up in a temple the spoils and armour of the slain, and supposes that here the people had suspended offerings on the pillars and porches in gratitude; both he and Robertson instance the golden vine with which Herod adorned the columns.

Clarke and Robertson both pause on the word for those offerings, and both make the same point about a single vowel. The noun for a thing consecrated and the noun for a thing accursed come from one verb meaning to set up or lay aside, and differ in writing only by the length of a vowel, so that the same root yields blessing in one form and cursing in the other. Robertson adds that the second word acquired its bad sense by usage rather than by derivation. Gill notices that two of the versions turn the reply into a question, asking whether these are the things the disciples were gazing at with such delight. Henry hears the whole exchange as a rebuke of misplaced admiration, and generalises it: when we speak of the temple it should be of the presence of God in it and the communion his people have with him there, and it is a poor thing when we speak of the church to dwell on its revenues and the dignities of its officers, the king's daughter being all glorious within. He notes too that the disciples expected their Master to be as much affected by the sight as they were.

The reply is absolute and the commentators keep its edge. Henry paraphrases it as a direct answer to the admiration just expressed: those dear things you are so much in love with will be so ruined that not one stone shall be left upon another, and some now living may see it. He draws out the double impossibility the disciples would have felt, that the building seemed too beautiful for anyone to pull down for pity and too strong for anyone to pull down by force. Clarke says only that it was literally fulfilled. Robertson attends to the grammar and finds the construction here slightly different from the two parallels, both in the case governed by the preposition and in the form of the negative, and he adds the human note that after the triumphal entry this must have come as a shock. Gill identifies the questioners as the disciples, observing that although the parallel names one of them there were evidently more, one perhaps opening the subject and the others joining him, and that the question was put later on the Mount of Olives rather than on the spot.
8:
Ellicott notes that the word Christ in the impostor's claim is supplied by the translators and that the sentence is better left in the vagueness of the Greek, the bare "I am" having already become significant without a predicate; he adds that the better manuscripts drop the closing charge not to follow them. Clarke glosses the claim as usurping the name and Wesley marks the whole sentence as the seducers' own words rather than the speaker's. Robertson derives the verb for being led astray from the root that gives us the word planet, and does not keep the warning in the past, calling it needed against the false cries of his own day; he adds that it is easy to forget the plain denial here and insist the end is immediate. Gregory explains why the troubles are announced in advance at all: they disturb less when they come if they have been foreknown, for darts strike the less which are foreseen. He divides the two nouns between the enemy without and the citizen within, so that the hearer is warned he will be troubled from both quarters, and observes that the last tribulation is preceded by many.

Much of what follows is peculiar to this Gospel, and Ellicott keeps a running tally: the word for commotions occurs in no other, the verb for being terrified only here and at the end of this book, the pestilences are its own in the best manuscripts, the phrase for fearful sights is its own, the clause marking persecution as coming before all the rest is its own, and the words about travail-pangs which the other two have are absent. He and Robertson both notice the same effect of sound, the nouns for famine and pestilence being all but identical in Greek and giving a rhythmical emphasis no English can carry over. Robertson adds that the participle for being haled away was a technical term of Athenian law, and that one scholar insists the priority meant is time, not magnitude. Gregory reads the order itself as the argument: first the hearts of men are disturbed and afterwards the elements, so that when the whole frame of things falls into confusion it may be plain from what retribution the ruin arises, the calamity arising not from injustice in the one who inflicts it but from the deserts of the world that suffers it.

On the promised mouth and wisdom, Gill takes the first as a faculty of speaking freely and Clarke as a ready utterance joined to an irresistible eloquence. Ellicott hears behind it the promise made to Moses when he drew back from speaking, and presses it further, arguing that a gift covering both the inward thought and the outward words tells against any distinction between an inspiration of thoughts and one of words, since men think through the medium of language. The assurance about the hair of the head is read as proverbial by Clarke, Barnes and Wesley alike, and Barnes adds a historical claim to match it, that no Christian is thought to have perished in the city's calamities, the community having withdrawn beforehand across the Jordan. Gill refuses that comfort in the bodily sense, since those addressed have just been told some of them would be put to death, and takes it that they should be no losers in the main. The closing sentence divides them further. Several report manuscripts reading it as a promise rather than a command, that by endurance you shall gain your lives; Ellicott prefers gaining to possessing, Wesley takes it inwardly of being master of oneself and superior to disquieting passions, and Calvin refuses the whole idea of safety, holding that we are bidden to be always exposed to death and that no man commits his soul to God rightly until he has learned to live each day prepared to die.
20:
Robertson puts the weight on a tense. The participle for being encircled is a present, so the warning is to act while the ring is closing and not after the city is shut; and he adds that the Christians did in fact leave for Pella in time. He meets the objection that such words could not have been spoken before the armies came with a short answer, that they could if predictive prophecy is possible at all, and notes that the noun for armies means properly a camp and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Gill records that three versions make it one army rather than several, which he identifies with the force Titus brought. Wesley reads the two halves of the following verse as a single practical instruction, that those inside are to get out before the retreat is cut off by the converging forces and those in the country are on no account to go in. Henry sets the whole passage in its perspective, that the destruction of the city would be a little day of judgment and a figure of the second coming, and would be the destruction of the world outright to those whose hearts were bound up in it.

Ellicott treats this section as paraphrase rather than transcript, noticing that the phrase about days of vengeance answers to the great tribulation of the other two Gospels and that the reference to what has been written is peculiar to this one; he thinks the report throughout has the character of a free rendering, such as an oral tradition variously remembered would produce. He adds that the word used here for distress is not employed in that sense by the other evangelists though it is by Paul, and that the description of falling by the sword has nothing answering to it in the parallels. Barnes and Wesley identify the writings meant with the prophets and particularly with Daniel, Barnes quoting the passage about the people of the prince who should destroy the city and the sanctuary. Gill takes the vengeance to be for the rejection of the Messiah. Robertson notes that the closing sentences of these verses are found in Luke alone, and that the Old Testament had long carried warnings of the same kind.

The numbers are given by three of them and they agree. Robertson, Clarke and Wesley all report about eleven hundred thousand dead in the siege and some ninety-seven thousand carried off, Robertson citing the historian by book and section while adding that the figure is surely an exaggeration though the true number must have been large. Barnes gives the same two totals and then presses the last clause into later history, arguing that the treading down has been long and oppressive, the city passing from Roman to Saracen to Turkish hands, and reaching for the ancient image of a conqueror setting his foot on the neck of the captive. Clarke observes that the land itself was sold by the emperor, and Wesley that the foundations were ploughed up and a heathen temple raised where the other had stood. What the closing limit means divides them. Ellicott takes it to promise a restoration and finds the same thought developed in the argument of Romans, where the fulness of the Gentiles is a distinct echo of this phrase; Robertson agrees only that a limit to the punishment is implied. Clarke ties the term to the conversion of the nations and admits he cannot say when. Lightfoot doubts the restoration is in view here at all, says he sees no great reason to think those times will be fulfilled before the end of the world itself, and declines to press his own conjecture further.
25:
Robertson works through the vocabulary of the terror. The noun for distress means anguish and occurs once elsewhere; the phrase for perplexity describes a man who has lost his road; the word for the roaring is the one that gives us echo, a reverberating sound; and the word for the waves is an old term for the swell of the sea. Barnes reports a proposal to render the word for earth as land and to confine the whole to Judea, and thinks there is some propriety in it; he glosses the distress as the anxiety of men who do not know what to do to escape, and passes on the Syriac rendering, perplexity or the wringing of hands. Clarke takes the roaring sea as a figure for the Roman armies that were to overrun the country, and would translate the following phrase as coming upon this land rather than upon the earth. Ellicott and Robertson both note that the verb for hearts failing means literally to breathe out the soul, Ellicott adding that it is used by this evangelist alone and is the sort of word that would come naturally to a physician, and that the state it describes matches the account of the tempest in Acts.

What the coming refers to splits them three ways, and none of them hedges. Robertson takes it of the second advent and reads the wording as deliberately unhurried, saying it will be not till then and that the time element is left purposely vague. Barnes keeps the whole passage inside the first century, so that the redemption drawing near means the end of Jewish power and a deliverance of the disciples from the persecutions of that country; Ellicott says the same of the word for redemption, that in its primary meaning here it points to the deliverance which followed the destruction of the city, when the Church was freed from what had been its most formidable danger, though he notes the term is otherwise characteristic of Paul. Augustine takes a third road. He argues that the prophecy is not fulfilled by the evils of his own day, since those fall alike on the good and the bad and are common to both kingdoms, and that the tribulation meant will belong to the Church troubled by the world rather than to those who trouble it; and he reads the seeing of the Son of man of a coming in which he comes now, in his members as in clouds, or in the Church as in one great cloud.

On the command that follows, the emphasis everywhere falls on its being consolation rather than warning. Gregory observes that having spoken against the reprobate the discourse now turns to comfort the elect, and reads the gesture inwardly: in scripture the head often stands for the mind, since as the members are ruled by the head so the thoughts are governed by the mind, and to lift the head is to raise the mind toward the joys of the country above. His paraphrase is the plainest thing in the entry, that when the buffetings of the world multiply the hearer should rejoice, because when the world whose friend he is not draws to its close, the redemption he seeks is near. Calvin makes the same point from the structure of the discourse, that the joy of the godly had to be set against the general sorrow so that they should not view the coming with horror, and notes that scripture describes the same judgments quite differently according to whether it addresses believers or unbelievers. Ellicott adds that the verb for looking up occurs only here and in one other place in this Gospel, and Robertson that it is used here of the soul where the other instance is of the body. Wesley reads the whole as looking up with firm faith and lifting the head with joy.
29:
Two of them notice that the fig tree is not alone here. Robertson observes that where the other Gospels keep to that one tree this one adds all the trees, which is true of them all though the fig was the commonest in the country; Ellicott takes the addition as a mark of the occasion, since the words were spoken just before the Passover when the spring was visible in every grove, and thinks they were suggested by what the disciples could see from the mount where they sat. He recalls that one such tree had lately been found in full leaf. Wesley says the same in a sentence, that it was spring and the trees on that hill were budding. Robertson adds two small points of vocabulary, that the verb for shooting forth appears only here and in one place in Acts, and that the season named is summer and not harvest. Wesley makes something of the phrase about knowing it of yourselves, that no one needs to teach it, and Henry builds the comparison out: as in nature there is a chain of causes, so in providence one event follows on another, and a nation filling up the measure of its iniquity may be known to be near its ruin.

What the nearness of the kingdom means is read two ways. Clarke and Wesley both take it of the removal of the old order to make room for the new, Clarke saying that after the destruction of the Jewish state the doctrine of Christ crucified would be preached everywhere and everywhere prevail, and Wesley that the fall of the city, the temple and the religion was to make way for the advancement of that kingdom. Robertson denies that the beginning is meant at all and refers the words to the consummation. Ellicott simply notes that this Gospel paraphrases where the others have the barer form, that it is near, even at the doors. Henry reads the inference as a rule for reading providence generally, that when the ruin of persecuting powers is hastening on we may conclude the kingdom is near, since it gains ground once the opposition to it is taken away.

The saying about this generation is the hardest sentence in the chapter and Robertson says so outright, reporting that the words give critics a great deal of trouble. He lays out the positions without adopting one. Some apply them to the whole discourse, the fall of the temple and the second coming and the end of the world together, and of those some conclude that the speaker was simply mistaken in his expectation while others hold that he has not been accurately reported. Others confine the words to the destruction of the city, which did happen within that generation; and Robertson allows the force of this, granting that it is not easy in so long an eschatological discourse to tell where the one subject ends and the other begins. He closes by passing on a solution offered by another, that the destruction of the city is meant, but regarded as the type of the end of the world. Wesley takes the narrower view without qualification, referring all things to what had been said of the fall of Jerusalem in answer to the question first asked. Clarke glosses the phrase as this race of men and refers the reader elsewhere; Gill notes that the Oriental versions read all these things here; and Robertson observes that the negative attached to the promise is the strongest the language affords.
34:
Robertson and Ellicott both note that the word for surfeiting belonged more or less to medical vocabulary, Robertson glossing it as the nausea that follows a debauch and comparing the Latin term for the giddiness of too much wine. Ellicott treats the whole warning as another stretch with nothing answering to it in the parallel reports, and therefore as paraphrase; he lists what is peculiar in it, that this evangelist alone uses the words for overcharged and for surfeiting, and that he and Paul alone use those for drunkenness, for the cares of this life, and for unawares. He observes that the passage falls in with a tendency of this Gospel to record whatever warned men against sensuality and worldliness. Clarke keeps the physical image, that the word means literally to be made heavy as those are who have eaten or drunk too much, and turns it at once into counsel not to be rendered secure by an improper use of lawful things. Wesley asks the sharper question, whether the apostles themselves needed warning against such gross sins, and answers that if they did then no one is wise who thinks himself out of the reach of any sin.

Augustine reads the two dangers allegorically and against a Jewish practice, taking the cares of this life to answer to the winter of the parallel warning, mournful as winter is, and the surfeiting and drunkenness to answer to its sabbath, since a day given to worldly pleasure buries the heart in luxury while a spiritual sabbath is lost. On the snare, Barnes explains the figure from fowling, a net sprung quickly on birds that are not expecting it, and notes that the parallels use the flood in Noah's day for the same suddenness; Ellicott adds that the word is absent from the other Gospels though Paul has it several times. Clarke and Wesley both narrow the scope of what follows, Clarke rendering the phrase as the face of this whole land and referring the judgments to Judea, and Wesley glossing those who sit upon it as the careless and those at ease. Robertson takes the command to watch as the pith of the whole warning, deriving the verb from being sleepless and reading the aim as standing before the Son of man without dread, which he says is the goal.

On what standing before him means, Barnes takes it of approbation and acquittal, the opposite of the condemnation coming on the city, and Wesley of standing with joy and triumph rather than falling as his enemies fall; Ellicott notes the better manuscripts read having strength to escape rather than being accounted worthy, and Wesley that the word for worthy sometimes means an honour conferred and sometimes merely what is fitting. Clarke would attach the phrase for continually to the watching as well as the praying, holding that no man is safe at any time who does not take the advice as literally as possible. The closing verses draw out the daily pattern. Ellicott explains that the word for lodging meant strictly to pass the night not in a room but in a courtyard, and was used in military language for a bivouac, which suits the accounts that most of those nights were spent in a garden rather than a house. Bede makes the example the point, that the one who bid us watch and pray was himself instant in teaching, watching and prayer as his suffering drew near. Cyril observes that the people heard him gladly because he spoke with authority, applying to spiritual worship what had been delivered in figures, and that those who came before light might fitly say that early they waited upon God. Barnes and Wesley both press the rising: he did not waste his mornings, and his hearers were happier at those early lectures than the morning slumber could have made them.
